name: Luke
author: From early times the church has named Luke as the writer: a doctor and travelling companion of the apostle Paul, who mentions him in his letters. He was probably a Gentile (not Jewish), well educated and writing in polished Greek, and he also wrote the book of Acts as a second volume. He was not an eyewitness of Jesus' life but gathered accounts from those who were. Many accept this tradition, though others think the author was an unknown later Christian, perhaps connected with Paul's circle.
audience: Luke addresses his work to Theophilus, probably a well-placed patron or official, possibly a new believer. Behind him stood a wider circle of mostly Gentile Christians spread across the Roman Empire, many of whom had never seen Judea. They wanted a careful, orderly account of the faith they had joined.
era: Jesus lived under Roman rule, when Judea and Galilee were governed by Roman officials and local kings from Herod's family. Luke wrote decades later, as the church was spreading from Jewish communities into Greek-speaking cities across the empire. Traditionally the book is dated to the early 60s AD, though many scholars place it around AD 80–90, after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

notes.1:1: This formal opening follows the style Greek historians and writers of the day used when dedicating a work to a patron.
notes.1:5: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until about 4 BC; priests served at the temple in rotating groups, and offering incense was a rare, lot-chosen honour.
notes.2:1: Augustus was Rome's first emperor; scholars debate how this census fits with Quirinius's known census of AD 6 and Herod's death around 4 BC.
notes.2:21: Jewish law required a mother's purification offering about forty days after a birth; the two-bird offering was the option allowed for poorer families.
notes.2:41: Jewish families travelled to Jerusalem each spring for Passover; at around twelve a boy was nearing the age of taking on adult religious duties.
notes.3:1: The fifteenth year of Tiberius is around AD 28–29; Pontius Pilate governed Judea about AD 26–36, while Herod Antipas ruled Galilee.
notes.4:14: In a synagogue Sabbath service, scripture was read aloud from scrolls, and a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.
notes.4:31: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, and it became Jesus' base during his work in Galilee.
notes.5:1: The Lake of Gennesaret is another name for the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake whose fishing trade supported the towns around its shore.
notes.5:17: Pharisees were a respected lay movement devoted to strict keeping of God's law; teachers of the law were experts who studied and explained it.
notes.5:27: Tax collectors gathered tolls and taxes for Herod Antipas or Rome, often overcharging, so they were widely despised as cheats and collaborators.
notes.7:1: A centurion was a Gentile officer commanding around a hundred soldiers, here probably serving Herod Antipas in Capernaum.
notes.7:11: Nain was a small village in southern Galilee, a few miles from Nazareth.
notes.8:26: The region of the Gerasenes lay across the lake in largely Gentile territory, which explains the herd of pigs, animals Jews did not keep.
notes.9:7: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and had imprisoned and executed John the Baptist.
notes.9:10: Bethsaida was a town near where the Jordan River enters the north end of the Sea of Galilee.
notes.9:51: Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea; they and Jews had centuries of bitter disputes over worship, and pilgrims to Jerusalem were often unwelcome.
notes.10:25: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho dropped steeply through lonely desert for about seventeen miles and was notorious for robbers.
notes.10:38: John's Gospel places the home of Martha and Mary in Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem.
notes.13:1: This killing of Galileans by Pilate is not recorded elsewhere; the tower of Siloam stood near the Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem.
notes.17:11: People with skin diseases were required by law to live apart from others and keep their distance, often in small outcast groups.
notes.18:35: Jericho was a lush oasis city about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem as the crow flies (a little farther by the winding road), a usual stop for pilgrims on the way up to the city.
notes.19:1: Jericho sat on a busy trade route, making it an important tax post where a chief tax collector could grow very rich.
notes.19:11: Listeners may have recalled Herod's son Archelaus, who travelled to Rome around 4 BC to be made king while a Jewish delegation opposed him.
notes.19:28: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, the ridge facing Jerusalem from the east across a valley.
notes.19:45: In the temple's outer court, traders sold animals for sacrifice and changed money into the coins required for the temple tax.
notes.20:20: Paying the Roman tax was a bitterly divisive question; the denarius, a silver coin, carried the emperor's image and title.
notes.20:27: The Sadducees were a wealthy priestly party linked with temple leadership who did not believe in a resurrection of the dead.
notes.21:5: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple on a grand scale around 20 BC; the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.
notes.21:20: Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70; scholars differ on whether Luke wrote before or after this event.
notes.22:1: Passover recalled Israel's escape from Egypt and ran into the week-long Festival of Unleavened Bread, when Jerusalem filled with pilgrims.
notes.22:63: The council, often called the Sanhedrin, was the Jewish ruling body of priests and elders, led by the high priest.
notes.23:1: Only the Roman governor could order an execution; Herod Antipas was in Jerusalem for Passover, and only Luke records his part in the trial.
notes.23:26: Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in modern Libya, with a large Jewish community whose members came to Jerusalem for festivals.
notes.23:32: Crucifixion was a public Roman execution used mainly for slaves and rebels, carried out outside Jerusalem's walls at a place called The Skull.
notes.23:50: Wealthy families used tombs cut into rock, sealed with a stone; burial had to be hurried because the Sabbath began at sunset on Friday.
notes.24:13: The exact site of Emmaus is uncertain; it lay about seven miles from Jerusalem.
notes.24:50: Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem.
